archetype.name: Playoff Team (goalie-and-finishing driven)
archetype.definition: A good team, with a real goaltender and a modest 5-on-5 chance edge, whose 7-2-0 start is inflated by shooting and save percentages near the top of the league.

report.headline: A real playoff team riding percentages it won't keep all season
report.take:
Boston opens at 7-2-0, second on the site, with the league's second-best goal differential per game (1.67) and a five-game win streak where it outscored opponents 25-8. Every roster group grades an A. The record isn't built on close-game luck either: Pts vs Goal Diff is slightly negative (-0.7), and only one win needed overtime. On the scoreboard this has been a team winning by margin.

The margin rests on percentages. Boston's skaters are shooting 14.8% in all situations, second in the league against a league average of 11.3%. Its goalies are stopping .929, third. Add them together and all-situations PDO is 107.8, second in the league, with 5-on-5 PDO at 106. The shot counts tell a quieter story. Boston gets 25.4 shots a game (23rd) and allows 28.2 (24th), and it owns only 49% of 5-on-5 shot attempts. The Bruins are being outshot and winning comfortably anyway, which happens when the puck goes in at an unusual rate at both ends.

There is more to it than luck. The 53.1% xGF share ranks 11th, so Boston creates better chances than it allows even while giving up volume. That is a sharp turn from last season's 47.3%. Jeremy Swayman is the other real piece: .934 and 6.6 GSAx over seven starts, third on the goalie tab, and last year's team led by its goalies at 30.6 GSAx. Strong goaltending has now held up across seasons. A 14.8% shooting rate has not. Pastrnak (12 points, 34 shots) is driving the attack, and depth centers like Minten (four goals, +7) and Hagens (six points in under 13 minutes) are contributing more than their minutes suggest.

The 128-point pace is a nine-game artifact. Expect the shooting percentage to fall and the scoring with it, and expect the shot deficit to start costing games once the save percentage is merely good. What remains is still a playoff team: a positive chance share, a goalie with a track record, and a power play converting 25%. It is not a team that will keep winning by nearly two goals a night.

strengths.title: Swayman is carrying again
strengths.body: Swayman has a .934 save % and 6.6 GSAx in seven starts, and the team's 8.3 GSAx ranks third. Unlike the shooting numbers, this has a track record behind it: last season's goalies saved 30.6 goals above expected. The save % will come down from .929, but Swayman is the most sustainable part of the hot start.

strengths.title: Chance quality improved from last year
strengths.body: Boston controls 53.1% of 5-on-5 expected goals, 11th in the league and up from 47.3% last season. It is getting the better looks even while being out-attempted. That gives the hot start a real base rather than pure variance, though nine games is too few to treat it as settled.

strengths.title: Pastrnak and a productive power play
strengths.body: Pastrnak has 12 points on 34 shots, five of them on the power play. The unit is converting 25%, ninth and well above the league's 20.4%. Last year's 23.4% suggests the power play is a genuine skill and not a fluke.

concerns.title: Shooting percentage will not hold
concerns.body: The skaters are shooting 14.8%, 3.5 points above the league average and second overall, which pushes all-situations PDO to 107.8. No team sustains that, and the five-game burst of 25 goals is where most of it came from. Expect goals per game to drift down noticeably from 3.78.

concerns.title: Outshot at both ends
concerns.body: Boston is 23rd in shots for and 24th in shots against, and it holds under half the 5-on-5 attempts. While the goalie stops .929 and the shooters hit 14.8%, that doesn't matter. Once the percentages normalize, a team allowing more shots than it takes gives back much of that margin.

concerns.title: Penalty kill is merely average
concerns.body: The PK is killing 81.3%, 15th, only modestly above the league's 79%. Last year it sat at 77%. It isn't a weakness yet, but it isn't the edge the goal-against ranking implies.

trend.note: Two straight regulation losses to Minnesota and Ottawa in early October gave way to five consecutive wins in which Boston scored five goals a game and allowed 1.6. The run is the high point of a percentage surge, not a new baseline.

weekAhead.headline: Two winnable home games bracketed by Dallas and Carolina
weekAhead.body:
The week splits cleanly. It opens in Dallas against the league's stingiest defense and best save percentage. Nashville and San Jose follow at home, both beatable, and the week closes in Carolina against the site's top team. Taking points at home is the expectation, especially against a San Jose side Boston beat 6-3 a week ago that ranks 29th in xGF %.

The road games are the real test of the shot-volume question. Dallas allows only 22.4 shots a game with an A+ goaltending group, so Boston's 14.8% shooting runs into a .944 save percentage. Carolina takes 33.1 shots a game and holds 60% of attempts, exactly the kind of opponent that exposes a team allowing 28.2 shots. A 2-2 or 3-1 week is a fair read.

keyMatchups.title: Hot shooters meet Dallas's wall
keyMatchups.body: Dallas leads the league in save % at .944 and has held opposing forwards furthest under their expected points. Its own offense ranks 27th, so goals will be scarce at both ends. This game shows whether Boston's finishing holds up against elite goaltending.

keyMatchups.title: Carolina's shot volume vs Swayman
keyMatchups.body: Carolina takes 33.1 shots a game, second in the league, behind a 58.6% xGF share. Boston already allows more shots than most teams. Expect Swayman to face a heavy workload and decide the result.

keyMatchups.title: San Jose's soft spot on the wing
keyMatchups.body: San Jose lets wingers score above expectation, 24th in the league by that measure, and its goalies sit at .877. That suits Pastrnak and Peterka. Nashville's 29.6% power play is the one special-teams danger of the home stand against an average Boston PK.

weekAhead.watch: Boston's shots against in Dallas and Carolina: if it is buried in volume and still wins, Swayman is the story; if not, the percentages are starting to turn.

restOfSeason.body:
From here, the shooting percentage should fall toward league norms and the team save percentage should drift down from .929, while the shot deficit stays roughly where it is. That combination moves Boston from a nearly two-goal-a-game differential to a modest positive one. The 53.1% xGF share and a proven starter keep it on the right side of the ledger, so this still projects as a solid playoff team in a tight Atlantic, not the 128-point juggernaut its pace suggests.

The sustainable parts are Swayman, a productive power play and a better chance share than last year. Expect regression in the 14.8% shooting, the 2.11 goals allowed a game and the five-goal nights. A finish of roughly 95 to 106 points is the reasonable band, higher if the chance-share gain is real and Swayman stays near his current level.

projections.stat: Goals allowed / game, rest of season

swingFactors: Whether Swayman stays near elite save rates
Whether the xGF % gain over last season holds
Closing the shot-volume gap at both ends

confidence.note: Nine games, and the percentages are extreme, but goalie history and chance share support a playoff-level baseline.
